Alright, let me think through this season. I've got 5 mu of land here in Quzhou, and it's the same plot I've been working for 35 years. My son and daughter-in-law both work at the garment factory in town, so they're not always around when I need them. It's mainly me and my wife handling the farm day-to-day, though my son comes back for the big rush in June when we harvest wheat and plant maize — that window is brutal, usually less than a week.

**Winter wheat:** I'll plant around October 10th, same as always. The soil's gotten a bit tired over the years, but I know these fields. Last year I got about 420 kg per mu on the wheat, which was decent. The extension guy at the agricultural station said 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I've been doing this long enough to know that with my land, if I go a bit under, the wheat turns yellow at jointing and I lose yield. So I'm putting down about 25 kg per mu of compound fertilizer before planting — the kind with 28-6-6 on the bag. Then at jointing, if the wheat looks a little pale, I'll topdress another 10 kg of urea per mu. That puts me around 14-15 kg of nitrogen total. It's a bit more than the book says, but I'd rather waste a few yuan on extra fertilizer than have a bad year. We need that wheat for our own flour, and whatever we sell helps with my granddaughter's school fees.

For irrigation, I'll water three times: once before winter to help establishment, once at green-up in March, and once at jointing. The well water isn't free — the electricity for pumping keeps going up — but three times is what my neighbors do, and if I skip one, the yield drops too much. I'll use flood irrigation; it's what my equipment allows.

Pesticides — I'll spray herbicide in early spring for the weeds, and keep an eye out for rust. If I see aphids, I'll spray insecticide, but I won't do it preventively. That's money I can save.

**Summer maize:** The wheat comes off around June 8th-10th, and I need that maize in the ground by June 15th at the latest. I don't have my own combine, so I'll hire Old Wang's machine — 50 yuan per mu. After harvest, there's no time for proper plowing. I'll hire someone with a rotavator to chop the wheat stubble and loosen the top soil, then plant right away. For seed, I buy hybrid seed from the supply shop. I used to save my own seed, but the hybrid stuff really does yield better — about 450-480 kg per mu when things go well. Seed costs me around 30 yuan per mu.

For fertilizer, maize is less demanding than wheat in my experience. I'll put about 20 kg per mu of compound fertilizer in the furrow at planting, then topdress with 8 kg of urea per mu when the plants are knee-high. That's around 11 kg of nitrogen per mu total. The extension people say you can go higher, but maize responds well enough and I need to watch my cash. I only irrigate twice for maize — once if it's dry right after planting, and once at the big trumpet stage in August. Some years we get enough rain in July that I can skip the first one, but I'll budget for two.

For pests, maize always gets some weeds, so I'll use herbicide. And I keep a close eye on the corn borer — if I see the signs, I'll spray insecticide immediately. Last year I caught it early and saved the crop.

**Labor and costs:** My wife and I do most of the work — spreading fertilizer, irrigating, spraying. For wheat planting and maize harvest, my son helps when he can get time off. But for the June rush, I might need to hire one worker for a couple of days to help with carrying and planting. Hired labor is 120 yuan per day now, so I keep it to a minimum.

The biggest constraint is cash. Between seeds, fertilizer, pesticide, irrigation electricity, and hiring the combine, I'm looking at spending most of what I set aside from last year's sales. I keep a small reserve for emergencies — my wife insists on it — so I can't push inputs to the maximum even if it might give a bit more yield. This farm is about keeping us fed and stable, not getting rich.
